complete_before_row: 2.2 Fix a Euclidean metric in one link chart and transport it through the similarity charts. The metric is independent of the transport path, because every loop has identity linear holonomy and translations preserve the Euclidean metric. This gives a global flat metric $g_v$ on the compact torus $T_v$, hence a complete one. Its lift to the universal cover is complete as well: any geodesic projects to a geodesic on the complete torus, extends there, and the extension lifts through the covering. The lifted Euclidean charts develop to a local isometry into $\mathbb R^2$. Every finite straight segment starting at a point in the image lifts to its endpoint: a partial lift has finite length, is therefore Cauchy, and extends from its limit by the local isometry. Hence the development is onto. For a small Euclidean ball about any point, lifting its radial segments from each preimage gives disjoint isometric copies of that ball; lifting the reverse radial segments shows these copies exhaust its preimage. Thus the development is a covering, and since $\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected it is an isometry. Deck transformations have identity linear part by the trivial link holonomy, so act by translations. Compactness of $T_v$ makes their translation vectors a rank-two lattice $\Lambda_v$. The assembled end is therefore the quotient of a horoball by $\Lambda_v$, with metric $dr^2+e^{-2r}g_v$ in horospherical depth $r$. A path escaping toward the ideal vertex has length at least the change in $r$, so the end is complete. Repeating this argument at each of the finitely many vertices proves completeness at every end. Connected coordinate arcs cover $\Gamma$; compactness gives a finite subcover, so $\Gamma$ has finitely many connected components. By [F5] each component is a smooth embedded circle. Put the planar $k$-component unlink, $k\ge1$, in its standard $k$-bridge position: the upper and lower balls each contain $k$ boundary-parallel arcs with the same noncrossing matching of their $2k$ endpoints. Its double cover is two balls joined by $k$ one-handles; the first joins the two zero-handles, and each remaining handle adds one genus. Thus it is a genus-$k-1$ handlebody. Doubling each of its $k-1$ co-core disks gives disjoint nonseparating two-spheres. Cutting them removes those one-handles and leaves a sphere with paired ball holes; regluing the pairs gives $\#^{k-1}(S^2\times S^1)$. For $k=1$ it is the double of a ball, hence $S^3$. complete_before_row: 1.3 For the knot-group comparison assume $L=K$. Let $\Gamma$ be the finite planar graph obtained by taking the crossings as vertices and the strand pieces between consecutive crossings as edges. Choose disjoint small disks about the crossing vertices, each meeting $D$ only in its two transverse branches, and disjoint tubular strips around the compact edge pieces outside those disks. At a crossing, oriented local coordinates straighten the branches to two transverse axes. Choose a nearby rational point and two rational direction vectors, still transverse and in the same cyclic order as the original branches; the four rational half-segments give the coded crossing and its over/under choice. Extend each edge strip a short distance into its endpoint disks through the corresponding disjoint branch sectors, and choose rational bend ports there. In each strip choose a simple rational polygonal path that is a graph in strip coordinates and joins its ports; choose it fine enough that rounding its bends gives a small normal graph over the original edge. If there are no crossings, choose a simple rational polygon in a tubular annulus of the projected circle. Since there are finitely many compact edge pieces, nonincident pieces have positive separation, and each crossing is transverse; density of $\mathbb Q^2$ and a sufficiently fine finite subdivision therefore let all vertices and bends be rational while preserving the one-circle tracing, crossing cyclic orders, orientations, and over/under data, with no other intersections. The resulting record is a valid code by [F4]; smoothing its bends in disjoint disks gives a smooth regular diagram with the same crossing data by [F6]. To compare it with $D$, move each crossing point to its nearby rational point by an isotopy supported in its disk and the short branch sectors, fixed at the outer ends of the strips, and interpolate its four half-branches, within their disjoint sectors, through transverse direction pairs to the rational branches. This is an isotopy preserving the cyclic order and over/under choice. After these local adjustments, each rounded edge replacement is a sufficiently small normal graph $r=f(s)$ over the original edge in its strip, with $f=0$ at the ports. Choose the approximation so $|f|\,\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$ for a cutoff $\chi$ that is $1$ near the edge and $0$ near the strip boundary. Then $(s,r)\mapsto(s,r+t\chi(r)f(s))$, $0\le t\le1$, is a diffeomorphism in each strip, fixed at its boundary, and gives an ambient isotopy of that edge. These finitely many disk and strip isotopies paste to a compactly supported ambient isotopy of the plane. Its product with the identity in height carries a lift of $D$ to a realization of the code diagram, so the code represents the same knot $K$. The induced bijection on under-arcs preserves source, target, and overarc at each crossing because the positive over-normal and branch orientations are preserved. This finite construction uses no choice axiom. [F4, F6, construct]

complete_before_row: 1.1 We first justify using bridge spheres for the height-based minimum in [F1]. In the product of regular height levels $S^2\times(-1,1)$, a maximum can be raised without changing the number or kinds of critical points: take a small cap containing only that maximum, perturb its horizontal location so that its central vertical ray misses the rest of the knot, narrow the cap inside its original small chart to fit a tube about that ray, and lift it along the ray, lengthening its two descending ends monotonically. The horizontal location is available arbitrarily close to the initial cap: the projection of the remaining finite collection of compact smooth arcs has empty interior, as follows by covering each arc by finitely many intervals of derivative bound $C$, whose projected images lie in disks of radius $C\delta$ and have total area tending to zero as $\delta\to0$. Compact disjointness then gives a narrow tube about the ray avoiding the rest of the knot; its two thin parallel sides are the lengthened ends. A horizontal cap perturbation and the subsequent vertical move have embedding tracks with no new extrema; the moving cap has the translated local quadratic maximum and the ends have strictly positive or negative height derivative. Extend with [F7]. Do this finitely many times, choosing distinct rays avoiding earlier cap tracks, until all maxima lie above a regular level above all minima. The upper and lower pieces are trivial tangles with simultaneous disjoint spanning disks: sweep their endpoints between successive critical heights, extending the finite point motions on each level sphere by disjoint small coordinate vector fields. Transport disjoint joining arcs by these level isotopies. At a cap choose its joining arc in its small cap chart, away from the finitely many earlier arcs (move those arcs off that chart by a level isotopy before the birth). Their swept traces, capped at the extrema, give pairwise disjoint disks. Conversely, for any smooth bridge sphere and displayed disks, [F6] first carries the sphere to a regular level. Push each bridge through its own disk to a thin collar of its foot; in disk parameters use a positive rounded arch whose height is $\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ above, and $-\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ below, with compatible endpoint collars. The disjoint same-side disks allow these isotopies simultaneously; [F7] extends them, and rounding at endpoints gives exactly one maximum per upper arc and one minimum per lower arc. Thus the minimum number of upper arcs over bridge spheres is exactly the height-defined $b$. In particular a minimum-height representative supplies a bridge sphere with $b$ upper arcs, and any factor bridge sphere with $n$ upper arcs gives $b(\text{factor})\le n$. [A1, F1, F6, F7, construct]
